factors.factor: Untested new code path: the Service Control quota policy checks were rolled out region by region but never exercised, because the path only triggers on a policy change, so the defect (null pointer on blank fields) went undetected until production.
factors.evidence: "This code change and binary release went through a region by region rollout, but the new code path was never exercised during this rollout because it needed a policy change to trigger it."

factors.factor: Insufficient validation and defensive handling of policy data: a policy change with unintended blank fields was accepted and replicated, and the consuming code did not handle blank fields, causing a null pointer crash loop.
factors.evidence: "This policy data contained unintended blank fields... This pulled in blank fields for this policy change and exercised the new code path, which hit a null pointer and caused the binaries to go into a crash loop."

factors.factor: Global, near-instant replication of regional policy metadata with no staged or canary propagation, allowing a single bad change to reach every region within seconds and causing the crash loop to occur simultaneously in every regional deployment, making the blast radius global.
factors.evidence: "This metadata was replicated globally within seconds." | "This occurred globally, in each regional deployment."

factors.factor: Recovery was slowed by a herd effect when restarting Service Control tasks overloaded the underlying Spanner table in larger regions, requiring throttling and traffic rerouting.
factors.evidence: "as Service Control tasks restarted, it created a herd effect on the underlying infrastructure it depends on (the Spanner table), overloading that infrastructure."

factors.factor: Mitigation depended on a red-button kill switch that had to be deployed manually and took about 40 minutes to roll out, delaying recovery.
factors.evidence: "Within 40 minutes of the incident, the red-button rollout was completed, and recovery started across regions"

factors.factor: Dependency of the status/communication infrastructure (Cloud Service Health) on the same failing Google Cloud infrastructure delayed customer notification by about an hour.
factors.evidence: "The first incident report was posted to Cloud Service Health ~1h after the start of the crashes, because the Cloud Service Health infrastructure was down due to this outage."

action_items.action: Require every new code path, including dormant or policy-triggered paths, to be exercised by automated tests with representative and malformed policy data before regional rollout begins.
Add strict schema validation and required-field checks on policy data at write time in the Spanner tables, rejecting changes with blank fields before they are replicated.
Make Service Control consumers handle null or blank policy fields defensively so malformed data degrades to a safe default instead of causing a crash loop.

Implement staged, canary-based propagation of policy and metadata changes so a change reaches a small set of regions first and is halted automatically if error rates rise, instead of replicating globally within seconds.
Replace the manually deployed red-button kill switch with an automated or pre-deployed mechanism that can disable a serving path within minutes, and test it regularly.
Add restart backoff, jittered startup, and load-shedding for Service Control tasks so that mass restarts do not overload the underlying Spanner table in large regions.
Host Cloud Service Health and status-publishing infrastructure on systems independent of Google Cloud's production control plane, so incident communication is not blocked by the outage it reports.
Define a target for initial customer incident notification and enforce it through paging and escalation rules for the communications team, so that the first public notice is not delayed by an hour.
Add alerting on crash-loop rates and 503 error spikes per region that fires within minutes of onset, so the on-call team is paged before customer-visible impact spreads.
Document and run recovery drills for large-region herd effects and multi-region database failover, including us-central1, to shorten time-to-recovery for future incidents.
